pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): naming and recognising the common minibeasts a child actually meets — ladybird, ant, bee, butterfly, spider, snail, worm, woodlouse, caterpillar, beetle.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 Y1 'Animals, including humans' (identify and name a variety of common animals); Y2 'Living things and their habitats' (identify that most living things live in habitats). Working-scientifically: identifying and classifying, using observation.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 1-LS1-1 (external parts) and 2-LS4-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1] an area) by building the vocabulary and recognition base those depend on.
• Operational details — recognition is a naming/vocabulary goal: match a real image to its everyday name, notice one or two salient recognition features per creature (ladybird = red with spots; snail = shell; woodlouse = grey armour plates). Foster POSITIVE attitudes to all minibeasts, including the ones children find 'yucky' (spiders, worms). Use real photos or lifelike illustrations, not cartoons that distort features.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): points to and names 4-5 common minibeasts from pictures. Tier B (age 6): names 8-10 and gives one recognition feature for each. Tier C (age 7): sorts a mixed set correctly by name and explains the feature they used ('I know it's a spider because it has 8 legs').
bestPractices: Anchor each name to ONE or two unmistakable recognition features (spots, shell, number of legs, wings) rather than long descriptions — recognition at this age is feature-cued.
Use real photographs or lifelike illustrations; cartoon minibeasts distort the very features (leg count, body segments) children need to recognise.
Deliberately include the 'unloved' minibeasts (spider, worm, slug, woodlouse) and model calm, curious, caring language to build positive attitudes and counter fear/disgust.
Connect naming to first-hand encounters — name the creatures the class found on a real bug hunt, so the vocabulary is grounded in experience.
Revisit names in low-stakes, repeated, playful ways (I-spy, guess-who, sorting) to move words into long-term recall.
keyRepresentations: A labelled field-guide gallery: one clear photo per minibeast with its name and a highlighted recognition feature.
Recognition-feature callouts (arrow to the ladybird's spots, the snail's shell, the spider's 8 legs).
A 'who am I?' silhouette/reveal pairing name to shape.
commonMisconceptions: 'All small crawly things are insects/bugs' — children lump spiders, worms, snails and insects together under one word; naming is the first step to later distinguishing them.
'Spiders are insects' — a very early and sticky error; at this stage just note spiders have 8 legs, insects have 6 (formal grouping comes at 7-9).
'A caterpillar and a butterfly are different animals' — children don't yet know they are life stages of one creature (addressed in the metamorphosis topic).
'Minibeasts are dirty/dangerous and should be squashed' — an attitude misconception worth naming and gently correcting.
Confusing look-alikes: centipede vs millipede, bee vs wasp vs hoverfly, slug vs worm.

learn.summary: For 5-7 year olds, naming and recognising common minibeasts (ladybird, ant, bee, butterfly, spider, snail, worm, woodlouse, caterpillar, beetle) by anchoring each name to one or two unmistakable visible features, grounding the vocabulary in first-hand encounters, and deliberately building warm, curious attitudes toward the 'unloved' creatures as well as the pretty ones.

activities.title: Explore-the-garden field guide: tap, name, and say how you know
feedback: When the child names a feature, affirm the specific one: 'Yes — those shiny, spotted wing cases tell you it's a ladybird.'
If they count 8 legs on a spider, prompt: 'You counted 8 — a spider has eight legs; insects like the ant have six.' If they get a different number, count the legs together slowly.
For a less popular creature, model warm curiosity: 'The woodlouse has little armour plates — what do you think they are for?'
If they say a feature that isn't reliable, redirect to a countable or unmistakable one (legs, shell, wings).
activities.rationale: Recognition at this age is widely treated as feature-cued, so anchoring each name to one or two salient visible features and asking the child to justify the name ('how do you know?') is intended to support durable recognition. Real photos or lifelike illustrations are used rather than cartoons, because cartoons distort leg count and body segments — the very features children need. These are proposed pedagogical choices, not measured outcomes.
learnerActions: Explore a photo-real garden or park scene (leaf, flower, log, soil, wall) and find the minibeasts hiding in it.
Point to or tap a creature to reveal its everyday name, with an arrow highlighting the recognition feature (ladybird's spots, snail's shell, spider's legs, woodlouse's armour plates).
Before the answer is shown, answer the prompt 'How can you tell it's a ____?' yourself, then check against the revealed feature/fact.
Look under the log to find the woodlouse and worm, and at the web to find the spider — 'count its legs!'.
Zoom in on any creature to look closely at its features.
Name at least six minibeasts and, for each, say one visible feature that identifies it.
activities.intendedInsight: Each creature is a NAMED creature with a reason you can point to — turning a vague 'creepy-crawly' into 'I know it's a snail because it carries its shell' or 'it's a spider because it has 8 legs'.

activities.title: Bug hunt: name the creatures you actually find
feedback: Name the creature with the child: 'That's a woodlouse — see the grey armour plates.'
Model calm, curious, caring language for creatures children find 'yucky': 'Worms help the soil — let's put it back gently.'
Celebrate curiosity about less popular creatures as much as butterflies.
activities.rationale: Connecting naming to first-hand encounters grounds the words in experience, and deliberately featuring the unloved minibeasts with warm modelling is intended to counter fear/disgust and build even-handed interest.
sourceClaims: Building positive attitudes toward invertebrates and grounding minibeast naming in first-hand outdoor encounters supports engagement and recognition at KS1.
learnerActions: Go on a real minibeast hunt outdoors (under logs, among leaves, on walls) and find living minibeasts.
Name each creature found, using the field-guide features as a reference.
Record or point to one recognition feature for each creature met.

Observe the 'unloved' creatures (worm, woodlouse, slug, spider) closely — gently handling the ones that are safe to hold, such as worms and woodlice, and observing spiders without handling — using calm, caring language.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary is grounded in real experience, and every minibeast — pretty or not — is interesting and worth naming and caring about.

activities.title: Playful recall games: match, I-spy, guess-who
feedback: On a correct match, restate the cue: 'Right — the shell told you it was a snail.'
On a mix-up of look-alikes (bee/wasp, slug/worm, centipede/millipede), draw attention to one distinguishing feature.
Keep it light and encourage re-tries rather than marking 'wrong'.
activities.rationale: Revisiting names in low-stakes, repeated, playful ways is a common practice for supporting movement into long-term memory. Active recall and immediate feedback reinforce recognition; a matching or sort task can check classification but does not by itself elicit the child spontaneously naming a feature, so it complements rather than replaces the reveal-and-name teaching.
learnerActions: Match name cards to the correct photos.
Play 'catch the ladybird' / I-spy: tap or point to the named creature in a busy scene.
Play 'who am I?' from a silhouette or revealed feature, then name the creature.
Sort a mixed set of photos by name and say the feature used to decide.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated low-stakes retrieval is intended to move the names and features into long-term recall.

activities.title: Meet-the-minibeast: a creature introduces itself (optional)
feedback: Echo the feature back: 'Yes, the woodlouse has armour plates.'
activities.rationale: A light in-character introduction may build warmth toward unloved creatures. Keep it to authored facts and a short introduction rather than open-ended questioning, since the goal at this age is naming and recognition, not extended dialogue.
learnerActions: Listen to a friendly minibeast introduce itself and its feature ('I'm a woodlouse — I have armour plates').
Repeat the name and point to the feature mentioned.
activities.intendedInsight: A warm first-person introduction may build affection and make the recognition feature more memorable.

constraints: Use real photographs or lifelike illustrations; cartoons distort leg count and body segments that children need to recognise.

Deliberately include the 'unloved' minibeasts (spider, worm, slug, woodlouse) with calm, curious, caring language to build positive attitudes and counter fear/disgust; building affection is an explicit goal, not an extra.
When handling live creatures on a bug hunt, limit hands-on holding to safe-to-hold minibeasts (e.g. worms, woodlice, snails) and keep spiders to close observation; always return creatures gently.
Keep any character 'meet the minibeast' voice to authored facts and a short introduction, not open Q&A, to avoid going beyond the naming goal.

Multiple-choice/matching checks (e.g. 'which one is the woodlouse?') confirm recognition but do not by themselves elicit the child spontaneously naming a feature; pair them with tasks where the child states the feature aloud.

At this age keep to a simple observation: spiders have 8 legs, and insects such as ants, bees, ladybirds and beetles have 6. A caterpillar also has 6 true legs; the stumpy 'legs' further back are not true legs. Woodlice, with 14 legs, are neither spiders nor insects. Formal grouping/classification comes later (around 7-9); do not require it here.
A tap-to-reveal picture guide is a strong scaffold for recognition but is strengthened by real bug-hunt encounters, which ground the vocabulary in experience.
Never present the misconception 'a spider is a kind of insect' as a valid option; use it only to shape corrective feedback via the countable 8-vs-6 legs contrast.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all listed sources remain marked verified:false and were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

sourceClaims for activity[0] were set to [] because the KS1 source claim supports the naming/curriculum topic but does not directly support the feature-cued-recognition or cartoon-avoidance teaching principle stated in that rationale.

The source treats a ladybird as a kind of beetle and expects children to accept this; the shared feature (hard wing cases lifting to reveal wings) is retained. This is biologically correct but is a subtle idea for age 5-7 — present it as an observable feature, not a required classification.

The source states 'naming and 2D recognition gain nothing from a 3D space' and that a quiz 'only assesses'. These comparative/universal claims are not established by the evidence and have been softened: a quiz/matching response format can be used during teaching, and recognition is simply well-served by clear visuals. No universal necessity or medium superiority is asserted.

The diagnostic correct answer, error patterns, and distractors from the assessment field were kept as teaching feedback cues but not copied as learner-facing truth claims beyond the simple 8-legs-vs-6-legs observation. The distractor 'a spider is a kind of insect' is a misconception and is never offered as a valid answer.
Caterpillar/butterfly as life stages of one creature is flagged in the source as a misconception addressed in a separate metamorphosis topic; not taught here.
Efficacy wording was softened to intended/may/supports where the sources establish curriculum requirements and practice conventions but not measured outcomes.

probeDeeper: A woodlouse isn't as pretty as a butterfly — is it still worth learning about? Why?
What could you count to check whether a creature is a spider?
How is a bee different from a wasp when you look closely?
assess.correctAnswer: The ladybird (a kind of beetle) has six legs and round red, spotted wing cases. The spider has eight legs, two body parts and no wings. Counting the legs or looking at the body shape tells them apart.

errorPatterns.pattern: They're all just 'bugs' — 'a spider is an insect too, same as a ladybird.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a countable feature — the spider's eight legs versus the ladybird's six — so the child sees they're different kinds.
errorPatterns.distractor: A spider is a kind of insect, just like the ladybird.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats spider and ladybird as the same kind of creature with no difference.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only the pretty minibeasts are worth knowing — 'worms and woodlice don't really count.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw curiosity to a woodlouse or worm — name it, find a feature, note its job — to build even-handed interest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses or refuses to engage with less popular minibeasts.

errorPatterns.pattern: A ladybird isn't a beetle — it's its own separate thing.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the hard wing cases lifting to reveal wings — the beetle signature a ladybird shares.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the ladybird is a beetle despite the shared wing-case body plan.

responseLevels.gap: Can't name the creatures or lumps everything together as 'bugs.'
responseLevels.full: Names each and gives a reliable distinguishing feature (legs, wings, body shape), showing curiosity across the range, not just the pretty ones.
responseLevels.partial: Names the minibeasts but offers no feature that reliably tells them apart.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are a ladybird and a spider. Name each one, and tell me one thing you could look at to be sure which is which.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who lumps every crawly together as 'a bug' can't offer a distinguishing feature. A child who really recognises them names a reliable feature — legs, wings or body shape.
